title: Writing effective error messages on Mac: a guide for technical writers
metaTitle: Writing effective error messages on Mac: guide for technical writers
description: Learn to master writing effective error messages for your product. A guide for technical writers on Mac covering clarity, empathy, and user-centric design.
intro: Writing effective error messages requires you to shift from technical documentation to user experience design. You must explain what went wrong and how the user can fix it without causing frustration.
tldr: Focus on the user, not the system state.
Avoid technical jargon that confuses the end user.
Provide a clear, actionable path forward in every message.
Test your copy with real users to ensure clarity.
Use a consistent tone across your entire product interface.

blocks.text: Why writing effective error messages is hard

When you are writing effective error messages, you face a unique set of constraints. You have limited screen space and a user who is likely already annoyed. Technical writers often default to system logs or stack traces. This is the wrong approach for a user interface. You need to translate technical failure into human language.

The main issue is the gap between how developers think and how users think. Developers care about the specific error code. Users care about why their task stopped and how they can finish it. If you provide an error message that says 'Error 404: Object not found', the user is stuck. If you say 'We could not find that file, please check the folder path', you provide a solution.

items: Using passive voice that hides who or what caused the error.
Blaming the user with phrases like 'You entered the wrong data'.
Providing too much technical information that is irrelevant to the user.
Failing to offer a button or link to resolve the issue.

blocks.text: How to fix your error messages

Start by identifying the goal of the user. What were they trying to do when the error appeared? Once you know the goal, draft a message that explains the problem in one sentence. Then, add a second sentence that tells them what to do next. Keep it short. Use active verbs. Avoid jargon.
Use a tool like Marked 3 on your Mac to preview your copy. It helps you see how the text fits into a design layout before you finalize it.
blocks.title: Preview your work

blocks.text: You should not be working in isolation. If you are writing effective error messages, you need to be part of the design review process. Use Figma or Sketch to see the error modal in context. Ask the designer if the text box has enough room for your copy. If the space is too small, you need to edit further.

Do not wait until the final build to check your copy. If you see an error in the design file, fix it there. It is much cheaper to change a string in a design file than to update a production build later.

Validation is the final step. Show your error message to someone who is not a developer. Ask them what they would do if they saw this message. If they hesitate, your message is not clear enough. You need to revise it until the action is obvious.

faq.question: Should I include error codes in my messages?
faq.answer: Only include them if the user needs to provide them to support. Otherwise, keep them out of the main message.

faq.question: How long should an error message be?
faq.answer: Aim for two sentences max. One for the problem, one for the solution.

faq.question: What if the user made a mistake?
faq.answer: Avoid blaming. Focus on the solution. Instead of 'You made a mistake', use 'Please check your entry and try again'.

costs.title: User frustration
costs.text: Users stop using your product because they cannot resolve simple issues.

costs.title: Support tickets
costs.text: Vague error messages lead to more support emails and phone calls.

costs.title: Development time
costs.text: Fixing bad copy after a release is more expensive than getting it right early.

causes.title: Technical bias
causes.text: Writing from the perspective of the system rather than the user.

causes.title: Lack of context
causes.text: Writing copy without seeing how it appears in the final interface.

causes.title: Time pressure
causes.text: Rushing the writing process during the final stages of development.

fixes.title: User empathy
fixes.text: Always ask yourself if a non-technical user would understand the message.

fixes.title: Action-oriented copy
fixes.text: Include a clear next step in every error message you write.

fixes.title: Peer review
fixes.text: Have a colleague read your message and explain what they think it means.

plan.label: Morning
plan.title: Review existing copy
plan.text: Spend 30 minutes reading through your current error messages to identify the top three most confusing ones.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Draft improvements
plan.text: Rewrite those three messages using the user-first approach. Focus on action and clarity.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Test with users
plan.text: Show your new messages to someone outside your team and ask for their feedback.
